title: Holding chambers (spacers) versus nebulisers for beta-agonist treatment of acute asthma
authors: Cates CJ, Welsh EJ, Rowe BH
population: 39 randomised trials in 1897 children and 729 adults with acute asthma in emergency departments, community settings or hospital wards
funder: Internal sources: NHS Executive, North Thames, UK; NHS Executive Eastern Region, UK; Department of Emergency Medicine, University of Alberta, Canada; St George's University of London, UK. External sources: Garfield Weston Foundation, UK; Canadian Institutes of Health Research.
authorConflicts: The authors have no financial interest in any of the devices used to deliver beta2-agonists in acute asthma and no involvement with the primary studies.
result: Hospital admission did not differ between metered-dose inhaler with spacer and nebuliser: adults RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.43; 9 trials, n = 582), children RR 0.71 (0.47 to 1.08; 9 trials, n = 757). Children's stay in the emergency department was 33 minutes shorter with spacers (24 to 43), against a mean of 103 minutes with nebulisers. Pulse rate in children was lower with spacers (mean difference -5% of baseline, -8% to -2%), and tremor was less frequent (RR 0.64, 0.44 to 0.95; 4 studies in children). Peak flow and FEV1 were similar.
